summary:
HOSA is an interactive, science driven web platform that transforms NASA's lunar data into accessible insights for lunar exploration and preliminary mission planning. Focusing on the Moon's south pole, HOSA addresses a critical challenge: complex terrain and changing astronomical conditions can significantly affect sunlight availability and direct Earth visibility, making potential mission locations difficult to evaluate.

Our platform combines NASA LOLA elevation data with JPL/NAIF SPICE astronomical calculations to reconstruct lunar terrain, calculate terrain horizons, and analyze time dependent illumination and Earth line-of-sight conditions. Through interactive 3D visualization, users can explore the Moon, compare candidate sites, identify suitable operating periods, and evaluate mission requirements. An AI assistant helps explain scientific results, while a deterministic backend ensures transparent, evidence based calculations and explicitly identifies uncertainty.

HOSA bridges the gap between complex scientific data and practical understanding, empowering researchers, mission planners, educators, and space enthusiasts to explore lunar environments and make more informed decisions. Our vision is to advance toward spacecraft specific lunar landing site assessment and mission support.
details:
HOSA is an interactive, science driven platform designed to support lunar exploration and preliminary mission planning through real NASA data, geometric analysis, and 3D visualization. Our project focuses on the Moon's south pole, where low solar elevation and complex terrain create major challenges for sunlight availability and direct Earth visibility. Even nearby locations can experience significantly different conditions depending on the surrounding landscape and observation time. HOSA addresses this problem by helping users explore lunar terrain, evaluate environmental constraints, and compare potential mission locations through a single accessible web application.

At the core of HOSA is a scientific computation pipeline that combines Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) with astronomical information calculated using JPL/NAIF SPICE. We use terrain datasets with grid resolutions of 5, 80, and 240 meters to reconstruct the lunar surface and calculate terrain horizons. For each observation point, our algorithm scans the surrounding landscape to determine the highest blocking angle in different directions. These terrain horizons are then compared with the calculated positions of the Sun and Earth over time. Rather than treating the Sun as a single point, HOSA divides its apparent disc into 64 strips to estimate the visible solar area, providing a more detailed illumination model. The system subsequently calculates equivalent full-disc sunlight hours, Earth line-of-sight duration, darkness periods, and potential communication windows.

One of HOSA's key technical features is its explainable, uncertainty aware evaluation system. Users can define mission parameters such as observation location, start time, mission duration, equipment height, minimum sunlight requirements, and communication constraints. The backend evaluates these requirements and returns PASS, FAIL, or INDETERMINATE, accompanied by supporting metrics and validation evidence. Instead of assuming missing information is valid, HOSA preserves uncertainty and performs numerical consistency checks using different angular resolutions, scan distances, and time intervals. Selected astronomical calculations have also been compared with JPL Horizons reference data. This approach makes the results more transparent and reliable within the limitations of the underlying models.

To make these scientific capabilities accessible, we developed an interactive web interface that allows users to explore the Moon through Moon, Pole, and Ground views, select locations, adjust observation conditions, compare candidate sites, and search for suitable mission periods. An AI assistant supports natural language interaction and helps explain results, while the scientific calculations and decisions remain controlled by the deterministic backend. We built the frontend using React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Vite, and the backend using Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Pandas, Rasterio, PyProj, and SpiceyPy. To improve performance, we implemented reusable terrain horizon profiles, cached astronomical calculations, and indexed time-series metrics. Our default catalog contains 27 NASA entries representing 26 distinct coordinates, with four prepared observation height configurations and support for nominal metrics covering 2000 - 2100 when the required caches are available.

HOSA is designed to benefit three main user groups. For mission planners, it provides a practical way to screen potential locations, identify sunlight and visibility constraints, and prioritize areas for further investigation. For educators and students, it transforms complex lunar science into interactive experiments where users can observe how terrain, time, and observation height influence environmental conditions. For space enthusiasts, it offers an accessible opportunity to explore the Moon and understand scientific phenomena without requiring specialized technical knowledge. Our creativity lies not in replacing NASA's scientific tools, but in integrating authentic datasets, computational geometry, interactive visualization, uncertainty handling, and AI-assisted explanations into one coherent experience.

Our longterm vision is to develop HOSA into a more comprehensive lunar mission decision support platform. With additional information about spacecraft dimensions, landing systems, propulsion, surface slopes, obstacles, energy requirements, and communication capabilities, HOSA could eventually evaluate landing locations based on the specific characteristics and objectives of individual spacecraft. We also envision supporting more advanced mission simulations and recommendations for equipment placement and surface exploration. These are future development goals requiring additional physical models and validation. Ultimately, HOSA aims to bridge the gap between complex planetary data and meaningful decisions, making lunar exploration more accessible, transparent, and data driven.

NASA PGDA – LOLA lunar south-pole DEMs (20/80/240 m per pixel, error and hillshade rasters)
NASA PDS Geosciences Node – LRO LOLA Gridded Data Records (global LDEM_64)
NASA NAIF SPICE generic kernels (DE440 ephemeris, lunar frames, leap seconds)
NASA JPL Horizons System (Sun and Earth ephemerides seen from lunar sites)
NASA Moon Trek – LRO WAC/NAC imagery tiles (WMTS API)
NASA Moon Trek – Artemis III named south-pole regions layer
NASA Lunar Surface Data Book Rev A (ACD-50044) – Artemis candidate region coordinates
NASA Scientific Visualization Studio – CGI Moon Kit (LROC color map, LOLA elevation)
